name: Colorist
description: Samples the dominant colour of frames across a video and renders them as a vertical-stripe movie barcode, stored beside the media and shown at the foot of the detail page.

versions.changelog: Fixes the settings page buttons, which 0.3.2.0 left unstyled. Jellyfin's button theming keys on an attribute that release removed, so every button on the page rendered bare; the attribute is back on all of them, generated ones included. The tab strip along the top is now a row of tabs rather than a row of raised buttons, underlined to show which panel you are looking at, matching the Curator plugin's settings page.

Three fixes to the Run tab. The action buttons now match the Details and Hide buttons beside them: customized built-in elements do not upgrade when they are created from script, so the buttons in the run list had always been plain ones while the static buttons were not, leaving two kinds of button on one card. Run history recorded by earlier versions is now reordered too. Ordering by when a run started only applied to runs recorded after that change shipped, because older files are named by run ID alone and fall back to the time the file was last written, which is effectively when the run finished; those files are now read and renamed the first time the list is shown after an upgrade, so existing history sorts correctly as well. And a run cancelled by the user is now recorded as cancelled rather than failed. Generation spends its whole life inside the loop that hands items to workers, since that loop waits there whenever every worker is busy, so that is where cancellation actually arrives, and only the wait at the end was guarded; the cancellation escaped and the run was recorded with the failure message kept for a task that ends without reporting anything.

Adds control over how much of the machine a run uses, and fixes the run details list. A new slider on the Run tab sets the share of the processors Jellyfin can see that generation may take, defaulting to 25 percent, which is what the old fixed rule worked out to; the page shows what it resolves to as you drag it, for example 25 percent of 20 processors being 5 items at a time. One ffmpeg runs per item and each is capped at one decoder thread, so items in flight is close to cores in use, which is what makes a percentage meaningful. It is a budget rather than a hard ceiling: what holds the line when somebody starts watching something is the below-normal priority every ffmpeg already runs at, and this governs how much of an idle machine a run helps itself to. Typing a number into items at once still overrides it outright. In a container the share is of the CPUs Jellyfin has been given rather than the host's. Fixed: scrolling through a run's details snapped back to the top every couple of seconds, because refreshing the live figures rebuilt the whole list and destroyed the element being scrolled; the list is now patched in place and only rebuilt when its shape actually changes. Fixed: a run's details went permanently blank when that run finished while its drawer was open. Fixed: runs are now ordered by when they started rather than by when their file was last written, which is effectively when they finished, so a long run started earlier no longer sorts above a short one started later.

Every run now writes a log, and the settings page shows the live one as it happens. The Run tab carries a progress bar that updates every two seconds with what is being sampled right now, how far through the run is, how many items a minute it is getting through and how long is left. Under it, the last five runs are listed newest first; open one to see every item it touched, with the outcome, how long it took, how many frames were sampled and how many stripes those became, the crop that was applied, any HDR conversion, whether the barcode landed beside the media or in the plugin data directory, and the reason for anything that failed. Delete runs are recorded the same way, listing what was removed. The estimate is built from throughput rather than from an average item duration, because items are sampled several at a time and a mean would overstate the answer by the concurrency factor; it is measured over a recent window, so a run changing pace as it crosses from feature films into half-hour episodes is followed rather than averaged away, and it is measured against the current moment rather than the last completion, so a run stalled on one enormous file shows a growing estimate instead of counting down through a hang. Nothing is estimated until three items have finished, since the first two are mostly startup cost. Runs are kept in the plugin data directory and rotated at twenty. A run whose file still says running but has no process behind it, which is what a server restarted mid-run leaves behind, is reported as abandoned. Also fixed: the progress panel could fail to appear at all, because the page stopped polling the moment it saw an idle server and the task manager takes a moment to pick a queued job up, so the one poll after pressing the button landed in the gap and ended the loop just as the run began.

Barcodes are now stored as the colours that were sampled rather than as a picture of them. Each item gets a small JSON sidecar holding one packed hex triplet per stripe, about 6 KB for the default thousand columns, and the detail page draws the strip from that in the browser. Stripe blending and display height are applied when the page renders, so changing either costs a page reload instead of another ffmpeg pass over the whole library. The strip is fetched with a real Authorization header, so no access token travels in a URL, and an ungenerated item answers 404, which doubles as the existence check and halves the requests per page. Blended strips are interpolated perceptually in Oklab by the browser rather than through the dark seam plain sRGB blending puts at every transition. A PNG can still be written alongside the colour data, but it is off by default and nothing in Jellyfin reads it. New in this release: a Delete Barcodes scheduled task and a button on the settings page that remove what Colorist has written from library folders and from the plugin data directory, defaulting to clearing only the PNGs and keeping the colours. Fixed: the strip floated above the end of the detail page instead of sitting flush with it; the Letterboxing setting came back blank after every save and quietly wiped itself, because the value arrives from the server as a name rather than a number; the two dropdowns rendered white instead of taking the dashboard input colours; and the action buttons were full-width bars. The settings page now shows a title, the running plugin version and a description, with Save at the top of the form. Upgrading from 0.1: those barcodes are images with no colour data behind them and cannot be converted, so affected items will be sampled again on the next run.

The barcode now spans the full width of the detail page, edge to edge, at the height set in the plugin's settings. It is anchored to the page root rather than to the content container, which carries a 32.45vw left padding on wide layouts to clear the poster and would have indented the strip a third of the way across the screen; any padding on whichever anchor is used is measured and cancelled at render time, and re-measured on resize, because that padding is written in vw and percent and changes with the window. Selectors were taken from the stylesheet a real 10.11.11 server ships rather than guessed. The section heading is gone so the strip reads as a full-bleed band.

Fixes three problems found on a live server. The barcode image now displays: it is loaded by an img tag, which cannot send an Authorization header, so the endpoint answered every request with 401 and both the settings preview and the detail-page strip rendered as broken images — the access token now travels in the query string. Frame analysis is capped at the requested stripe count: -skip_frame nokey turned out to be only a hint, and a 110-minute 2160p film was delivering 157,791 frames for a 1,000-stripe barcode, so every frame was scaled and colour-clustered for nothing. HDR and Dolby Vision are converted before their colours are measured, rather than being decoded as though they were SDR — which read far too dark and far too grey, and made every 4K HDR title produce a muted strip. Dolby Vision profile 5, which has no HDR10 base layer and decodes pink and green, is converted with libplacebo so its metadata is actually applied; profiles 7 and 8 use the standard HDR path. If a required ffmpeg filter is missing, sampling falls back a step at a time and logs it rather than producing nothing.
